Hook: On the twenty-ninth of December 1967, in Washington, Milton Friedman gave his presidential address to the American Economic Association. Most of his audience believed that a government could choose from a menu: a little more inflation, and a little less unemployment, for as long as it liked. Friedman told them that there is always a temporary trade-off between inflation and unemployment, but no permanent one. Once people came to expect the inflation, the menu would vanish, and the unemployment would come back.

Here is what happened. America's unemployment rate across the bottom, inflation up the side, one dot a year. Through the 1960s the dots traced a neat curve: the menu. In 1969, unemployment was 3.5 percent and inflation 5.4. Then the curve came apart. By 1975, unemployment was 8.5 percent and inflation 9. In 1980, 7.2 percent unemployed with inflation at 13.5. Within a decade of the address, America had more inflation and more unemployment than at any time since the war.

This part's question: can a country buy lower unemployment with higher inflation? Why did the menu of the 1960s vanish? How do people form their expectations of inflation, and why do those expectations matter so much? And how do you bring inflation down once everyone expects it?
Economics, Built. Part twenty-eight: inflation and expectations.

Here is the plan. Phillips's curve, a forecast for you to make, and Friedman's natural rate. The Great Inflation, and two ways of modelling expectations. Lucas's islands, his critique of policy models, and inflation as a game a central bank cannot win. How Volcker ended the inflation, at what cost, and the institutions built to stop it returning. And the flat curve of the 2000s, the surge of 2021, two dials, the forecaster's job, and what surveys say about how people actually form expectations.
Curve: In 1958 Bill Phillips, the engineer of Part twenty-seven's water machine, published a curve. He took British unemployment and the growth of money wages from 1861 to 1913 and fitted this equation. It also fitted the years after the Second World War. Wages were stable when about five and a half percent of workers were unemployed. At two and a half percent, wages rose about 2 percent a year, roughly the pace at which productivity grew, so prices could stay stable. The tighter the labour market, the faster wages rose.

Two years later, Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow drew the American version for prices instead of wages, and turned it into a menu for policy. To keep prices stable, America would need five to six percent unemployment. To get unemployment down to three percent, it would have to accept prices rising four or five percent a year. And through the 1960s the economy marched up the menu, year by year, from high unemployment and low inflation in 1961 to low unemployment and rising inflation in 1969. Samuelson and Solow had warned that the menu might shift over time. That warning was the part most people forgot.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: forecast inflation.

Your turn. It is the end of 1972. Here is American inflation, year by year, from 1960. It crept up through the late 1960s, to almost six percent in 1970, then fell back, to 3.3 percent in 1972, under price controls. What will inflation be in 1973? About 3 percent, like last year; about 6; or about 11? Pause, and choose. Write your answer down: you will need it again.

In 1973, inflation was 6.3 percent. If you chose B, you were closest. The controls were lifted, and food prices jumped. In 1974, after the oil embargo, 11 percent. Hardly anyone looking at the 1960s would have guessed. Most people forecast by looking back, as you just did, and through the 1970s forecasts made that way kept falling behind. That is this part's subject: how expectations are formed, and what they do to the trade-off.
Natural: Friedman's argument, which Edmund Phelps had made a year earlier in a different form, starts with what people bargain over. Workers care about what their wages buy, and so do firms. So a wage deal builds in the inflation both sides expect. The curve becomes this: inflation equals expected inflation, minus a term in how far unemployment is from its natural rate. The natural rate is the unemployment that the labour market's frictions produce on their own, the search and matching of Part twenty-four. Unemployment can sit below it only while inflation runs above what people expect: only while they are surprised. So there is not one curve but a whole family, one for every level of expected inflation.

Watch it on the Island. The council decides to hold unemployment at 4 percent, a point below the natural rate of 5. Each point of unemployment below the natural rate adds 0.5 of a point to inflation, over what people expect. People expect whatever inflation they saw last year. In the first year inflation rises from two percent to 2.5. Next year people expect 2.5, so to stay surprised inflation must reach 3.0. Then 3.5, and on: after fifteen years, 9.5 percent, and still rising. Holding unemployment below its natural rate does not take high inflation; it takes accelerating inflation. If expectations learn more slowly, inflation climbs more slowly, but it never stops.

The lesson. In the long run the curve is vertical, at the natural rate: there is no permanent trade-off. In the short run, surprises move unemployment, but surprises cannot be kept up. So steady inflation buys nothing, and rising inflation buys a little, for a while. Economists later called the natural rate the NAIRU, the unemployment rate at which inflation does not accelerate. It is the number every central bank tries to estimate, and nobody can see directly.
Adaptive: The simplest model of how people forecast is the one you probably used. Adaptive expectations: each year, correct last year's forecast by a fraction lambda of last year's error. With lambda equal to one, you simply expect whatever happened last year. With a small lambda, your forecast is a long, slow average of the past. Phillip Cagan used it in his study of hyperinflations, in Part twenty-five, and your forecast for 1973 was probably some version of it.

How well does it work on America's inflation since 1960? In red, what happened. In gold, last year's rule: its typical error is about 1.8 points. In violet, a slow average, with lambda at a fifth: worse, 2.2 points, because it is always late. Worse still is the pattern. From 1966 to 1980, even last year's rule was too low, by 0.8 points a year on average; from 1981 to 1986, as inflation fell, it was too high, by 1.9. A rule whose mistakes run the same way, year after year, is one that nobody sensible would keep using. That was the opening for a very different idea.
Islands: If people forecast rationally, why would a surprise ever move output? Robert Lucas answered in 1972 with a parable. Producers live on separate islands. Each sees only the price of its own good. When that price rises, it might mean more people want this good. Then it pays to work harder and produce more. Or it might mean that there is more money everywhere, every price is up, and nothing real has changed. Then producing more is a mistake. Each producer has to guess which, from a single price. Economists call it a signal-extraction problem.

The answer depends on how noisy each kind of news is. A rational producer treats a share theta of any price surprise as real, where theta compares the variance of relative prices with the variance of money. On the Island, with two hundred producers and sixty years: when money is calm, output responds 0.79 to a money surprise, because a price rise usually means real demand. When money is wild, output responds only 0.10, because producers have learned that most price rises are just inflation. So the trade-off should be steepest where inflation is most volatile, and Lucas found that pattern across eighteen countries in 1973: in Argentina, with its wild inflation, demand moved prices and barely moved output.

Thomas Sargent and Neil Wallace drew the startling conclusion in 1975. If only surprises move output, then a monetary rule that eases after a bad year is foreseen, built into expectations, and surprises nobody. Systematic monetary policy cannot steady output at all; only random policy moves it, and that only adds noise. The result needs prices that adjust freely. Part thirty shows what happens when prices are set in advance, and policy works again.
Critique: Part four showed the Lucas critique with slowly adapting expectations. Here it is with rational ones. For forty years the council has aimed at 2 percent inflation, with random misses, and people expect two percent. Output rises whenever inflation is a surprise. An economist fits a line through the blue years: output rises 1.9 for every point of inflation. A clean, stable relationship. So the council moves its target to 6 percent, and the line predicts output of 108. But people now expect 6 percent, and output averages 100, exactly where it always was. The slope was a fact about the old rule, not about the economy. Change the rule and the relationship changes with it. That was Lucas's critique, in 1976, of every policy model of the day.

Lucas's paper was called Econometric policy evaluation: a critique. A model's coefficients summarize how people behaved under the old policy. But their decisions depend on what they expect policy to do. So to judge a new policy, you need a model of what people want and what they know, not a table of past correlations. That argument is the reason macroeconomics rebuilt itself, from the late 1970s, on people's tastes, firms' technology and everyone's expectations. Part twenty-nine is the first result.
Game: Chapter nine. Time inconsistency: inflation as a game.

Why did central banks let it happen? Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott in 1977, and Robert Barro and David Gordon in 1983, turned the question into a game. The central bank dislikes inflation, but it would also like output a little above its natural level, perhaps because taxes and monopolies keep the natural level too low. Its loss is half the square of inflation plus lambda times half the square of the gap between output and that target. Output rises above its natural level only when inflation surprises. On the Island, the bank wants output two above natural, and cares about output as much as inflation. The timing matters. The public forms its expectations, in wage contracts, first. Then the bank chooses inflation.

Play it forward. Suppose the bank promises zero inflation, and is believed. Then output sits at its natural level, and the loss is 2. But once wages are set, the bank is tempted: inflate by 1 percent, surprise everyone, push output up, and the loss falls to 1. The public can work this out too, so it never believes the promise. In equilibrium, expected inflation is exactly high enough that the bank has no reason to surprise anyone: lambda times b times k, 2 percent. Output is at its natural level anyway, and the loss is 4, double the rule's. All of the inflation, none of the gain. Nobody did anything irrational; the problem is that the bank cannot commit.

The lesson is about rules versus discretion. A rule the bank cannot break beats freedom to choose afresh each year, even for a bank with good intentions. Kydland and Prescott called the problem time inconsistency: the best plan made today is not the best choice when tomorrow comes. It is everywhere: a government that promises never to bail out banks, never to grant another tax amnesty, never to pay a ransom. The cure has to make the promise believable, and chapter eleven shows how central banks tried. Kydland and Prescott shared the Nobel prize in 2004.
Volcker: The cure came from Paul Volcker, chairman of the Federal Reserve from August 1979. Inflation, in red, peaked at 14.6 percent in 1980. On the sixth of October 1979, the Fed announced that it would target the growth of money and let interest rates go wherever that took them. The federal funds rate, in green, reached 19.1 percent in 1981. Two recessions followed, and unemployment, in blue, reached 10.8 percent at the end of 1982, the highest since the Depression. And inflation fell below five percent by 1983, and stayed there.

What did it cost? Here is America's output against the Congressional Budget Office's estimate of potential, quarter by quarter, from 1980 to 1985. Add up the shortfalls and you get about 16 point-years: as if output had been one percent below potential for 16 years. Over the same years, core inflation fell from 12 percent to 4. Divide one by the other, and you get a sacrifice ratio of about 2: two point-years of output for each point of inflation removed. Laurence Ball, measuring sixty-five disinflations, found that faster ones, and those in countries with more flexible wage-setting, cost less per point. If people believe the central bank, the cost should be smaller still. Whether they believed Volcker at first is doubtful: long-term interest rates stayed high for years.
Fixes: Chapter eleven. The fixes: conservative bankers, independence, targets.

Kenneth Rogoff proposed one fix in 1985. Appoint a central banker who cares less about output than society does. Add supply shocks to the Island's game, and plot society's expected loss against the banker's weight on output. A banker who shares society's tastes leaves the full inflation bias: a loss of 5.0. A pure inflation hawk, who ignores output entirely, removes the bias but lets every shock hit output: 4.0. The best appointment is in between: a banker with about 0.3 of society's concern for output, and a loss of 3.5. Conservative, but not fanatical.

The other fix is independence. Put the central bank out of the government's reach, so that nobody facing an election can order a surprise. Alberto Alesina and Lawrence Summers found in 1993 that rich countries with more independent central banks had lower inflation, and no worse growth or unemployment. It is a correlation: countries that wanted low inflation may also have been the ones that chose independence. Then came targets. In 1990 New Zealand gave its central bank a number, a deadline and a governor accountable for both. Canada, Britain, Sweden and dozens more followed, and the Federal Reserve named two percent in 2012. A target turns a vague promise into one the public can check, year by year.
Flat: Chapter twelve. The flat Phillips curve.

After Volcker, the curve flattened. Across the bottom, how far unemployment was from the Budget Office's estimate of its natural rate; up the side, how much core inflation changed that year. From 1960 to 1983, the slope was about -0.65: each point of extra unemployment took about two thirds of a point off inflation in a year. From 1984 to 1999, -0.18. From 2000 to 2019, -0.07: almost flat. In the Great Recession, unemployment rose five points above its natural rate, and inflation barely moved. Economists talked of the missing disinflation.

Why so flat? Three answers, all partly true. First, anchored expectations: once everyone expects two percent, prices and wages are set as if inflation will be two percent, whatever the slack. Second, good policy hides the curve: a central bank that offsets every shift in demand leaves no trade-off in the data to see. Third, the curve itself may be flatter, with global competition and fewer price changes. Jonathon Hazell, Juan Herreño, Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson got around the second problem by comparing American states, which share one central bank. They found the slope small, and small even in the early 1980s. If so, the great disinflation came mostly from Volcker changing what people expected, not from the slack he created.
Surge: Then, in 2021, the curve woke up. American consumer prices rose 9 percent in the year to June 2022, the fastest in forty years. Core inflation, without food and energy, peaked at 6.6. But the inflation expected over five years, read from the bond market, never went above 3.4 percent. The anchor held, and inflation came down without a recession.

Was the flat curve wrong after all? Measure slack differently: job openings for every unemployed person. From 2001 to 2020, in blue, core inflation sat near two percent whatever the ratio. In 2021 and 2022, in red, openings rose to about 2 for every unemployed person, and inflation rose with them. Pierpaolo Benigno and Gauti Eggertsson argued in 2023 that the curve is not a line but a hockey stick: flat while there are more unemployed than openings, steep once openings outnumber the unemployed and employers compete for workers.

Three accounts, each in its strongest form. Supply: Ben Bernanke and Olivier Blanchard decomposed the surge and found that at first most of it came from jumps in energy and food prices and from shortages in particular sectors. Demand: stimulus and savings built up in the pandemic met an economy that could not produce enough to keep up. A bent curve: the labour market was so tight that the Phillips curve became steep. They agree on more than they differ. Long-run expectations held. And the labour market's contribution, small at first, came later and lasted longer than the shocks.

Called it? In June 2021, the Federal Reserve's median projection had inflation, by its preferred measure, at 3.4 percent that year, falling to 2.1 percent in 2022, as the bottlenecks of the reopening cleared. Many forecasters agreed; the view was nicknamed team transitory. The measure rose 5.7 percent over 2021 and 6.1 percent over 2022. The Fed began raising rates in March 2022, and inflation fell to about 3 percent over 2023, without a recession. Wrong, as a forecast. The longer argument, about whether the anchor would hold, went the transitory side's way.
Dials: Chapter fourteen. The Dials: the slope, and the sacrifice ratio.

Two new dials. The first is the slope of the Phillips curve. Phillips's own wage curve, at three percent unemployment, has a slope of about minus one: a point less unemployment, a point more wage growth. Samuelson and Solow's menu for America implies about minus one point eight. This film's regressions, of the change in core inflation on unemployment against its natural rate, give minus point six five for 1960 to 1983, minus point one eight for 1984 to 1999, and minus point zero seven since 2000. The status: contested. Some of the flattening is real, and some of it is anchored expectations and good policy hiding the curve, and estimates across states suggest it was never as steep as the aggregate data made it look.

The second: the sacrifice ratio, the output lost for each point of inflation removed. Laurence Ball's estimate for America's disinflation of 1979 to 1983 is about one point eight. Gregory Mankiw's textbook calculation, turning the extra unemployment into output with Okun's law, gives about two point eight. This film's, against the Budget Office's potential, about 2.0. Contested, because each number depends on what you call trend output and trend inflation, and statistical estimates are so imprecise that their intervals include zero. The rough consensus: about two years' worth of a point of output per point, less if the cure is fast and believed.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: forecasting inflation, bargaining over wages.

A forecaster starts from one of the series' facts: inflation is persistent. In American data, this year's inflation and last year's have a correlation of 0.73. It was 0.81 before 1984, and 0.52 afterwards, once the anchor took hold. In theory, persistence comes from contracts that last a while, from pay and prices indexed to past inflation, and from expectations that look back. Agora's column waits for Part thirty, which builds prices that are set in advance, a few at a time.

And the forecast this part began with. Called it? In December 1967, Friedman said there was no permanent trade-off: holding unemployment below its natural rate would take ever faster inflation. In the decade that followed, inflation and unemployment both rose, from five and three and a half percent in 1969 to nine and eight and a half in 1975, and the stable curve of the 1960s vanished. Right. It is one of the few forecasts in economics that changed the textbooks as well as the policy.

The working forecaster's toolkit follows from this part. Core inflation as the trend, with energy and food treated as shocks that usually pass. Expectations, from surveys of households and firms and from bond markets. Slack, from unemployment against its natural rate, or from openings per unemployed person. And at the bargaining table, wage deals build in the inflation both sides expect, and some include cost-of-living clauses that raise pay with past inflation. Those clauses spread when inflation is high, as they did in the 1970s, and make it harder to bring down.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: how people really form expectations.

The models of this part make strong assumptions about expectations. Since the 2010s, economists have asked people directly. In gold, the median American household's expectation of inflation over the next twelve months, from the University of Michigan's survey, since 1978. In red, inflation over the previous twelve. The gold line follows the red one, with a lag: households extrapolate. Through the 2010s, households expected about 3 percent, while inflation averaged under two. Michael Weber and his coauthors show that households' expectations are high, widely dispersed, and driven by the prices they see most often, at the petrol station and the supermarket.

And firms? Olivier Coibion, Yuriy Gorodnichenko and Saten Kumar surveyed firm managers in New Zealand, the first country to adopt an inflation target. Most could not say what the target was, and their forecasts of inflation were far apart. In calm times, keeping track of inflation is not worth the trouble; economists call it rational inattention. So what central banks announce reaches people slowly, unless inflation is high enough to notice, which is when it matters most.

The questions still open. If expectations are not rational, which model of them should policy use? Could a central bank steer expectations by speaking to households in plain words? Is the Phillips curve flat, hidden or bent, and is the two percent anchor as safe after 2021 as it was before? And what is the natural rate of unemployment now, and how would anyone know?
